core: working definition: a credit report is a record of a person's credit history, kept by credit bureaus (attributed to CFPB)
what it contains: accounts, payment history, inquiries, and public records, each named and described in one line
who creates it: credit bureaus collect information submitted by lenders and other creditors
who sees it: lenders, landlords, sometimes employers; what each sees varies
checking your report: the U.S. right to a free copy every 12 months via the authorized channel (FTC/CFPB, stated as U.S. context)
errors: mistakes happen and can be disputed — honest note, no legal advice
honest framing: the report is the raw file; the credit score is the summary (credit-scores is a sibling topic)
supporting: the three nationwide U.S. bureaus: Equifax, Experian, TransUnion
reports from different bureaus can differ because each collects from different sources
checking your own report does not affect your credit score
adverse-action notices entitle the consumer to another free report within 60 days of a denial
landlords often use tenant screening reports built from rental history plus credit information
no company can legally remove accurate negative information
outOfScope: how credit scores are calculated and scored (sibling topic credit-scores)
credit card mechanics, fees, and usage (sibling topic credit-cards)
identity theft reporting and recovery (sibling topic identity-theft)
specific legal remedies or litigation (no legal advice)

claims.claim: A credit report is a record of a person's credit history — the accounts they have opened, how they have paid them, and related information — kept by credit bureaus (consumer reporting agencies).

A credit report typically contains personal identifying information, credit accounts (type, limit or amount, balance, payment history, open/close dates, creditor name), collection items, public records (bankruptcies, liens, foreclosures, civil suits and judgments), and inquiries (companies that have accessed the report).

Credit bureaus create reports by collecting and storing financial data submitted by creditors — lenders, credit card companies, and other financial companies; creditors are not required to report to every bureau.

Lenders use credit reports to decide whether to lend money and on what terms (including interest rates) and to monitor existing accounts; insurers, landlords, and providers of utilities, cable, internet, or cell phone service may also use them; employers may see a report only if the applicant agrees.

In the United States, federal law entitles consumers to one free copy of their credit report every 12 months from each of the three nationwide bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion), and AnnualCreditReport.com is the only website authorized to fill those free orders; a separate program lets consumers check each report once a week for free there.

Consumers have the right to dispute errors on their credit report; fixing an error generally means contacting both the credit reporting company and the company that provided the information, explaining in writing what is wrong and why, and including supporting documents.
Requesting your own credit report does not hurt your credit score, and the CFPB advises checking your reports at least once a year.
The three nationwide bureaus' reports for the same person can differ because each bureau gathers information from different sources, so consumers should review the report from each one.
No company can legally remove accurate, negative information from a credit report; only genuine errors can be disputed and corrected.

The credit report is the raw, detailed file of a person's credit history, while the credit score is a summary number derived from that file — two different products (the score is covered by the sibling topic credit-scores).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How often a U.S. consumer can get a free credit report.
positions: Federal law guarantees one free copy every 12 months from each nationwide bureau.
The three bureaus have also permanently extended a program allowing a free weekly check of each report at AnnualCreditReport.com.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson states both: the annual right is the legal baseline (attributed to FTC/CFPB), and the weekly program is presented as a separate, currently available extension — avoiding the error of claiming the weekly frequency is the legal entitlement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a credit report and a credit score are the same thing.
positions: Popular usage often blurs the two terms.
CFPB and FTC material treats the report as the underlying record and the score as a number derived from it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson teaches the report as the raw file and explicitly points to the sibling topic credit-scores for how the score is built.
